a:r.a:t: The motivation is that gasoline prices are familiar, visible, and volatile. Most people understand the impact of gas prices, but it is hard to look at a raw weekly table and get an intuitive sense of where prices may move in the short term.

In this dataset, the lowest historical national weekly price is about 94.9 cents per gallon, while the highest is about 5.107 dollars per gallon. The latest observation in my snapshot is 4.621 dollars per gallon for May 18, 2026. That range shows why this is a useful forecasting problem: the target variable can move a lot over time, and even short-term changes matter for planning.

The user problem I wanted to solve is not just "can we train a model?" It is "can someone interact with the model easily?" So the app lets a user select XGBoost or SARIMA, choose a forecast horizon, and get a chart and table back from the deployed model API.

My project objectives were three things: first, collect and process real public data; second, compare more than one forecasting approach; and third, deploy the app and API separately so the architecture looks like a real data product rather than a local script.
